headline: Pilbara Minerals rockets +7.9% on a stunning FY26 earnings beat, gold hits record highs above $4,696/oz, and Iran's stalled war dominates world headlines.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Huge day for PLS — the company reported FY26 results showing revenue surged 152% as lithium prices recovered, and management turned bullish on the price outlook while flagging expansion plans. The market loved it. This is exactly the kind of earnings catalyst that can re-rate a beaten-down miner.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG edged higher last night as analysts pointed to strong Q2 2026 earnings and continuing AI momentum supporting the valuation. Solid, steady move — no drama, just the market pricing in a healthy business.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft nudged up last night, consolidating after a big AI-driven earnings surge earlier this year. The stock is digesting recent gains — no new news, just steady holding ground.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped today, likely dragged by broader risk-off sentiment in emerging markets and ongoing uncertainty around Iran-US tensions which affect oil-exporting EM economies. Nothing structural — this ETF bounces around with global mood.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: A small dip today during a session where AI-related stocks were mostly flat. No specific news catalyst — just everyday volatility for a thematic ETF.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Barely moved last night. There's noise around GTA 6 gameplay footage leaking, with Take-Two pursuing legal action to identify the leaker — but a former Rockstar director called it a 'nothing burger'. No material impact on the share price.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: Tiny dip today, reflecting the slight softness in US markets from last night's session. The S&P 500 and NASDAQ were both modestly positive, so this is just rounding noise — nothing to worry about.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Quiet positive session for VDHG — the diversified nature of this ETF meant it absorbed today's mixed signals well and nudged slightly higher. Steady as she goes.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX surges +7.9% on blockbuster FY26 results
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals reported a 152% revenue surge in FY26 as the lithium market recovers, returned to profit, and management flagged bullish price expectations plus expansion plans. The stock is still -18.8% in the red overall for your position — but today's move is a meaningful sign the turnaround thesis is playing out. For a long-term holder, this is encouraging news. Sit tight and let the recovery continue.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX still 14.6% underwater — long-term patience required
watch_today.detail: The AI ETF dipped another 0.43% today and remains your biggest loss position at -$43 (-14.6%). There's no structural reason to sell — AI investment themes are multi-year plays and regulatory uncertainty (which is all over the news today) creates short-term noise. For a long-term buyer, this is a hold. If you have spare cash, a small top-up at these prices could make sense given the long runway for AI growth.

watch_today.title: Gold hits record highs — tailwind for resource holdings
watch_today.detail: Gold jumped 1.57% last night to $4,696/oz — a new record high. This reflects global uncertainty (Iran tensions, US political instability) driving investors into safe havens. While you don't hold gold directly, rising commodity prices generally support the broader resources sector, which is good context for your PLS holding and the ASX 200 more broadly.

watch_today.title: GOOG holding steady — AI momentum intact
watch_today.detail: Alphabet edged up 1.05% last night supported by strong Q2 earnings and AI tailwinds. Your GOOG position is +11.2% in the green. Nothing's changed with the long-term case — Google remains one of the dominant AI platforms globally. Hold with confidence.

watch_today.title: VGE.AX down 1.35% — emerging markets jittery on Iran news
watch_today.detail: Your emerging markets ETF slipped today as Iran-US tensions escalate and global risk appetite softened. VGE is still slightly underwater at -2.4%. This is short-term noise driven by geopolitical headlines — the long-term diversification case for emerging markets exposure remains intact. No action needed.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cut hopes growing — watch the AUD
watch_today.detail: HSBC economists are pointing to the latest jobs data as signalling the end of the RBA's interest rate hiking cycle. The AUD is already up 0.65% today to 71.66 US cents. A stronger Aussie dollar reduces the AUD value of your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) slightly, but it also signals a healthier domestic economy. Worth keeping an eye on this week.

world.summary: Iran dominates the global agenda today — the country's president floated a US memo as a potential off-ramp from a stalled war, while Iran's foreign minister hit back at new US sanctions threats and major new gas reserves were discovered. Meanwhile, concerns are mounting in the US about Trump and election integrity ahead of the midterms.

stories.title: Iran's president signals US memo could end stalled war
stories.why_it_matters: Iran's president has publicly said a US diplomatic memorandum represents the best available path out of a war that has stalled with no clear resolution. This is a significant signal — it suggests Tehran may be open to negotiation rather than escalation. For everyday people, a de-escalation in the Middle East would ease pressure on global oil prices and reduce the risk of a broader regional conflict that could affect energy costs worldwide.

stories.title: Iran's foreign minister dismisses US sanctions threats as 'desperate'
stories.why_it_matters: Even as Iran's president floated a diplomatic opening, the country's foreign minister called US threats of new economic sanctions 'desperate' — a defiant counter-message that shows Tehran is not negotiating from a position of weakness. This mixed signalling (one hand extended, one fist raised) means a deal is far from certain. New sanctions would likely push oil prices higher, which flows through to petrol costs for Australian drivers.

stories.title: Iran discovers major new gas reserves amid war-damaged energy sector
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has announced the discovery of significant new natural gas reserves even as its energy sector has been battered by war. This matters for global energy markets — if Iran can eventually bring these reserves online (conflict permitting), it could increase global gas supply and put downward pressure on energy prices long-term. It also gives Iran a stronger hand in any future peace negotiations.

stories.title: Trump's election integrity claims alarm experts ahead of US midterms
stories.why_it_matters: Experts and Democratic strategists are raising fresh alarms about Donald Trump's continued questioning of US election integrity, with growing concern about whether he might attempt to interfere in the upcoming midterm elections. Democrats and their allies are actively preparing contingency plans. US political stability has global consequences — markets hate uncertainty, and any serious disruption to US democratic processes would rattle financial markets worldwide, including the ASX.

stories.title: Oil drops 1.6% to $85.63/barrel
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil (WTI) fell $1.43 last night to $85.63 a barrel — a 1.6% drop. The decline comes despite Middle East tensions, suggesting markets are taking some comfort from Iran's diplomatic signals. For Australians, softer oil prices are good news: they feed through to lower petrol costs and ease inflation pressure, which in turn makes it less likely the RBA will need to raise interest rates further.

markets.summary: A solid session all round. The ASX 200 closed up 0.49% today to 9,103 — a healthy close. Last night on Wall Street, both the S&P 500 and NASDAQ gained 0.43%, GOOG and MSFT nudged higher, and gold hit record territory above $4,696/oz. The Australian dollar is firmer at 71.66 US cents. Oil softened despite Middle East tensions.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today — the local market pushed higher as commodity stocks benefited from gold's record run and lithium names like PLS surged on earnings.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: modest gains as tech held up and the market absorbed Middle East news without panic.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night: steady gains, with AI-related stocks broadly supportive.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Record high territory — gold is surging as global uncertainty (Iran tensions, US political concerns) pushes investors into safe havens.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil slipped despite Middle East tensions — markets may be pricing in some diplomatic progress on Iran.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar rose as traders increasingly expect the RBA's rate hiking cycle is over — good for domestic consumers, slightly reduces AUD value of US holdings.

politics.summary: The Albanese government is moving to override Queensland on AI data centre energy rules, the union movement is at odds with the Reserve Bank, and Australia's big banks are quietly hiking fees ahead of a looming card surcharge ban.

stories.title: Albanese to override Queensland on AI data centre energy rules
stories.why_it_matters: The federal government is set to step in and set national energy rules for AI data centres, overriding a defiant Queensland government that has resisted the Commonwealth's approach. As AI infrastructure booms, data centres are becoming enormous electricity consumers — the question of how they're powered (coal vs renewables) and who pays for the grid upgrades is a major policy fight. This matters for energy prices and Australia's broader AI ambitions.

stories.title: RBA rate hike cycle likely over, says HSBC — jobs data the key signal
stories.why_it_matters: HSBC economists are interpreting the latest Australian jobs figures as a sign that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has finished raising interest rates — meaning mortgage holders may finally be off the hook for further hikes. The AUD's rise today of 0.65% suggests traders agree. If the RBA is indeed done hiking, that's a relief for households with variable-rate mortgages and could support consumer spending.

stories.title: ACTU clashes with RBA over inflation and data access
stories.why_it_matters: The ACTU (Australia's peak union body) is in a public fight with the Reserve Bank, having cut off the RBA's access to their data after the RBA warned that high wage growth could re-ignite inflation. The unions argue wages need to rise to help workers keep up with cost-of-living pressures; the RBA worries it could push prices higher again. This tension is a core economic debate right now — it directly shapes whether interest rates stay where they are or move further.

stories.title: Big banks hiking fees and slashing rewards ahead of card surcharge ban
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's major banks are quietly raising account fees and cutting credit card rewards programs ahead of a looming government ban on card surcharges — the extra fee merchants currently charge for paying by card. The banks are effectively recouping that revenue from customers directly instead. For everyday Australians, this means your bank account could cost more and your rewards points might dry up, even as the surcharge at the checkout disappears.

ai.summary: The big AI story in Australia today is a political one — whether the Albanese government has the policy chops to handle the AI boom. Globally, attention is turning to AI regulation failures, a powerful new coding model, and what 'autonomous medicine' might mean for healthcare AI oversight.

stories.title: Critics say Albanese not up to the AI challenge
stories.why_it_matters: The Nightly is running opinion that the Albanese government lacks a coherent national strategy to deal with the AI revolution — and that its energy rules fight with Queensland is a symptom of a broader policy vacuum. As AI reshapes industries from healthcare to finance, getting the regulatory settings right (or wrong) will have real economic consequences for Australia. Your GXAI.AX holding makes this directly relevant.

stories.title: C-SPAN airs debate on AI regulation and containment failures
stories.why_it_matters: A major US public policy discussion aired on C-SPAN about cases where AI regulation has already failed — situations where AI systems caused harm that existing rules didn't prevent or catch in time. The debate is shifting from 'should we regulate AI?' to 'why isn't current regulation working?' This is a key risk for investors in AI-exposed stocks, as regulatory crackdowns could reshape business models quickly.

stories.title: Healthcare AI sandbox points to 'autonomous medicine' as next regulatory frontier
stories.why_it_matters: Regulators are testing 'AI sandboxes' in healthcare — controlled environments where AI can make medical recommendations under supervision — but the next big question is autonomous medicine, where AI makes diagnoses or treatment decisions without a human doctor signing off. This is the AI frontier that could most directly affect ordinary people's lives. How governments regulate it will determine whether AI becomes a trusted medical tool or a liability minefield.

stories.title: Ox Alpha emerges as a powerful new AI coding model
stories.why_it_matters: A new AI model called 'Ox Alpha' has emerged as a standout performer at writing and debugging computer code — competing with the best models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic. In practical terms, it means developers can now potentially use another powerful tool to write software faster and with fewer errors. Competition in AI coding tools is heating up, which is generally good for productivity but puts pressure on any company that's been making money selling coding AI as a premium product.

sport.summary: The Tigers pulled off the NRL upset of the year against the first-placed Roosters in Round 25. The AFL finals picture is taking shape with the Wildcard Round fixture revealed, and Joey Manu's return to the NRL via the PNG Chiefs is confirmed. Round 26 NRL kicks off Thursday with Broncos vs Storm at Suncorp.

stories.title: Wests Tigers stun ladder-leading Roosters with 79th-minute winner
stories.why_it_matters: Wests Tigers produced what's being called the upset of the 2026 NRL season, beating the first-placed Sydney Roosters with a try in the 79th minute. There's now a verdict being sought on a Roosters star following the match. The Tigers' win shakes up the ladder and finals positioning heading into Round 26, while the Roosters will need to regroup fast — they face the Dolphins on Saturday.

stories.title: Knights learn finals fate; ugly hip-drop tackle injures Sea Eagles star
stories.why_it_matters: The Newcastle Knights have learned their finals judiciary fate after Round 25, while a hip-drop tackle in the Sea Eagles vs another side's clash left a Manly star injured during what was described as a thrashing. Hip-drop tackles remain a major issue in the NRL — the league has been cracking down hard on them with automatic suspensions. The Sea Eagles, who face the Dragons in Round 26 at 4 Pines Park on Friday, may need to reshuffle their lineup.

stories.title: Joey Manu confirmed signing with PNG Chiefs — NRL return locked in
stories.why_it_matters: Former Sydney Roosters star Joey Manu has officially signed with the PNG Chiefs — confirming his return to the NRL. Known as '007' for his ability to play multiple positions, Manu is a marquee signing for the expansion franchise. Reports suggest rival clubs could get access to him even sooner than expected if the PNG side's season ends early. It's a huge coup for the Chiefs and for NRL expansion into Papua New Guinea.

stories.title: AFL Wildcard Round fixtures revealed — finals picture takes shape
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL has locked in the full schedule for the Wildcard Round — the extra knockout games played before the main finals series begins. Fremantle holds no fears for Hawthorn according to pundits, while Melbourne (Dees) are being called the biggest loser of Round 24. The Wildcard Round is do-or-die stuff — one bad game ends your season, which makes this week's results critical for several clubs on the bubble.

stories.title: Sydney Swans crisis deepens over fresh allegation
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Swans are dealing with a deepening off-field crisis, with a fresh allegation emerging today. The club is already under scrutiny and this adds to the pressure at a critical time in the season. No further details are confirmed yet, but it's a significant story for one of the AFL's highest-profile clubs heading into finals.
